sentences.t: The chronology in one pass.

PhonePe was incorporated in December 2015, acquired by Flipkart in April 2016, and its app went live on UPI (Unified Payments Interface, India's instant bank-to-bank payment rail) in August 2016 in partnership with Yes Bank.

Walmart took control through its Flipkart acquisition, the two companies separated fully in 2022 with PhonePe shifting its domicile from Singapore back to India, and in 2023 the company raised $850 million at a $12 billion pre-money valuation: $350 million from General Atlantic, $200 million from Walmart, and the rest from Ribbit, Tiger Global, TVS and a further General Atlantic cheque.
That domicile move matters to the IPO story: listing in India requires being Indian.

PhonePe's business starts with a simple fact: it is the front end for nearly half of India's instant payments, 45.4% of UPI volume and 48.7% of value in December 2025, ahead of Google Pay and Paytm, per NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India, the retail-body that runs UPI) data.

The merchant side is the strategic asset: over 4 crore merchants, many acquired through the soundbox, the speaker that announces each payment, a device on which industry sources tell Inc42 the company earns 80% to 90% margins.
But the engine has three speed limits, and each explains a piece of the IPO story.
First, UPI carried no merchant fee for a decade, so the highest-volume product earns almost nothing directly; payments still produced 88.5% of revenue in FY25, through adjacent charges.

Second, volumes are exposed to policy: the August 2025 ban on real-money gaming knocked UPI transaction volumes down 23% and values down 26% from July levels, and GST enforcement pushed some vendors back to cash (Inc42).
Third, share is drifting, 47.22% in June 2025 to 45.4% by December, still dominant, no longer growing.

The fee regime that could fix the economics is the new merchant discount rate (the fee merchants pay to accept a payment) framework: 0.4% on person-to-merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300.
Its rollout, originally due 15 October, is now deferred to 1 January 2027 (Indian Express).
For PhonePe the deferral cuts both ways: the revenue unlock slips past the planned listing window, but the company avoids a merchant-friction experiment in the middle of its IPO roadshow.
FY25 revenue rose 40.4% to ₹7,114.9 crore.

The mix is the story inside the number: payments grew 23% to ₹6,299 crore, a sharp deceleration from the 77% growth of FY24, while everything else more than tripled, financial services (lending distribution, insurance broking, the payment gateway) to ₹557 crore from ₹207 crore, and the new bets (Share.Market, Pincode, the Indus Appstore) to ₹57 crore.
Non-payments is now 11.5% of revenue; it was 5% a year earlier (Inc42).
The bottom line needs care, because PhonePe reports it two ways and both are true.

The reported net loss narrowed 13.4% to ₹1,727.4 crore, and the EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization, a proxy for operating cash profit) loss narrowed 54% to ₹413.6 crore, a margin of -6% against -18% in FY24 (Inc42).

Strip out employee stock-option costs, a non-cash charge, and the picture flips positive: adjusted EBITDA of ₹1,477 crore (from ₹652 crore), adjusted profit after tax of ₹630 crore (from ₹197 crore), the first positive adjusted EBIT at ₹117 crore, and free cash flow positive with ₹1,202 crore of operating cash flow (CNBC-TV18, Entrackr, IBJ).
The roughly ₹1,900 crore gap between the two versions is mostly stock compensation, which is real dilution for shareholders even though it is not cash.
One more number frames the whole journey: accumulated losses stood at ₹14,860 crore at the end of FY25 (Entrackr).
Lending is the intended profit engine.

PhonePe acquired an NBFC (non-banking financial company, a lender that cannot take deposits) licence in 2023, lends against its merchant transaction data, and has added secured loans against mutual funds.
The pitch: 4 crore merchants generate the underwriting data, so credit can be priced better than a bank's guess.

The reality check is relative: Inc42 cites PhonePe disbursing about ₹300 crore a month in mid-2024, against Paytm's roughly ₹5,000 crore a quarter, in a field that also includes BharatPe, Jio Financial and every bank app.
Around lending sit three smaller bets, each a use for the payments user base.
Pincode (April 2023) is a hyperlocal commerce app built on ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce, the government-backed open e-commerce protocol).
Share.Market (August 2023) is a stockbroking and mutual-fund platform, competing with the Groww and Zerodha machines this series has already torn down.
The Indus Appstore (February 2024) is a homegrown alternative to Google Play.
Together with financial services they are the 11.5% of revenue that is supposed to become the IPO's growth story (Inc42, Wikipedia).
The contrast that prices all of this is Paytm.

Paytm is less dependent on payments (58% of a ₹6,900 crore revenue), far ahead in lending, and back to net profit, helped by selling Paytm Insider to Eternal for ₹2,400 crore and its PayPay stake for $279 million.
PhonePe has the bigger engine and the weaker second act; the IPO asks public investors to fund the catch-up (Inc42).
The timeline tells the story.
PhonePe filed its draft papers confidentially in September 2025.

SEBI (the Securities and Exchange Board of India, the markets regulator) cleared the offer on 20 January 2026, and the public draft red herring prospectus, the offer document with everything except price and dates, followed.

The plan: about ₹12,000 crore, mostly an offer for sale (existing investors selling their shares rather than the company raising new money) by Walmart, General Atlantic, Ribbit, Tiger Global and TVS Capital.
Then, in March 2026, the company paused, citing global market volatility.
In September 2026, with the merchant-fee framework settled, the IPO was revived: a refile by the end of this year and a listing targeted for February-March 2027 (Inc42, Mint via Inc42, IBJ).
Three numbers in that paragraph deserve a second look.
First, mostly-OFS means the money goes to exiting investors, not into the business; buyers of the IPO are funding the 2023 round's exit more than PhonePe's next chapter.

Second, the valuation talk has compressed: the 2023 private round priced PhonePe at $12 billion pre-money, Inc42's September 2025 feature floated $12-15 billion IPO hopes, and the September 2026 revival reports a target near $10 billion.
Third, the March pause and the revival bracket exactly one variable, market conditions, which is the one thing the company does not control and the thing the February-March 2027 window is betting on.
UPI concentration: 88.5% of revenue touches payments, so every UPI policy decision, fees, caps, gaming rules, is a PhonePe earnings event.
The gaming ban's 23% volume hit is the worked example.
The fee deferral: the 0.4% merchant fee now starts 1 January 2027, weeks before the targeted listing.
The first full quarter of fee revenue lands after the roadshow, so the IPO prices the promise, not the proof.
Lending is late and crowded: Paytm disburses roughly five times PhonePe's monthly volume, and banks are in the same merchant-credit market.
Valuation drift: $12 billion private in 2023, $10 billion targeted for 2027.
A further market wobble between refile and listing reopens the March question.
What to watch: the refiled DRHP (due by year-end per Inc42), monthly NPCI share data, the 1 January 2027 fee go-live, and any change to the February-March 2027 window.

How this teardown was sourcedFinancials are from Inc42's feature and Entrackr's and CNBC-TV18's analyses of PhonePe's FY25 annual report; the IPO timeline from India Business Journal and Inc42's September 2026 report; the chronology cross-checked against Wikipedia and PhonePe's own draft prospectus.
Adjusted figures exclude stock-option costs and are labelled as such.
Vendor-adjacent claims (soundbox margins, disbursement run-rates) are attributed to the sources that reported them.
